newsitem.title: FRANCE: French budget deficit down 21 bln Fr y/y mid-April.
newsitem.headline: French budget deficit down 21 bln Fr y/y mid-April.

text.p: French government spokesman and budget minister Alain Lamassoure said in a newspaper interview published on Friday that the state budget deficit was 21 billion francs lower on April 17 than at the same stage a year earlier.
"As for the state budget, the deficit, on April 17, was down 21 billion francs versus the same period last year," Lamassoure said in an interview in Le Parisien newspaper.
He did not give the actual figure for the deficit, only the difference compared to the same time a year earlier.
The government has yet to release complete official figures beyond the end of February.

Lamassoure reiterated that the government would achieve its goal of reducing the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year, a target figure for for the European monetary union, and that improving growth should then allow it do even better.
"I think we can soon bring the deficit back to two or 2.5 percent of GDP," he said, without giving any indication on the scale of timing he was referring to for this.
The official government forecast is for three percent this year and 2.8 percent in 1998.

On the government budget deficit, official finance ministry figures released on April 15 showed the deficit at 72.4 billion francs by the end of February, 17.6 billion francs less than the 90 billion franc deficit at the end of February 1996.
As the centre-right government heads into a parliamentary election on May 25-June 1, ministers have been more generous with more up-to-date, if not formal, figures on the deficit.

Prior to Lamassoure's remarks, the latest indication came from Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on April 18, when he told a press briefing: "The first elements we have for March point to an improvement of around 18 billion (francs) over last year".
Lamassoure said in the Parisien interview that people should stop blaming Europe for the deficit reduction drive, saying France's deficit was the fault of the preceding Socialist government.

"Let's stop saying it's because of Europe that we're obliged to cut our deficits. It's because of the Socialists. In the five years following German reunification, state spending rose faster in France than in Germany," he said.

On this year's goal of reducing the public deficit to three percent of GDP, Lamassoure said: "Let's stop rambling on about slippage. The state budget and the social security budget are under control".

There has been intense press speculation in recent weeks that the government will be forced to make extra spending cutbacks this year to reach its deficit goal and impose even more stringent measures to keep the deficit down in 1998 to respect its single currency requirements.
